title: The Hidden Tech Behind Everyday Devices: Norma's Journey into Embedded Systems

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Hi everyone. Welcome again to another episode of TechPeeps Diaspora. Today my guest is Norma. She's an embedded systems engineer, and I'm gonna hand it over to Norma to briefly introduce herself. Hi Norma, how are you doing?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Hi, my name is Norma. Um, I'm an embedded systems engineer. I've been doing this for 2 years now. Actually, it was 2 years, 3 days ago. Embedded systems is really a thing that I'm really passionate about, so I'm excited I have this opportunity.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Nice. Uh, yeah, I have a vague idea of what embedded systems engineering is. Um, and I think maybe similar for other people. Uh, what exactly, uh, is embedded systems engineering? Um, what do you do, um, on your day-to-day job?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Embedded systems engineering is in I guess the simplest way I can put it is it's like a mashup between software engineering and then electrical engineering and sometimes mechanical engineering. On a day-to-day, you work with systems, you work with controllers, you work with software that tells hardware what to do, essentially. So embedded systems exist in most systems that are smart and most systems that are able to do multiple tasks that are still related to the same thing, like a washing machine. Yes, it tells you how long it's been going. It tells you how much water is in the washing machine and everything, but all these individual tasks come together so that you can have something washed and possibly dried as well. So it's a focus between designing how this system or this machine should be able to accomplish whatever task, and then what software that machine is going to relate to, to be able to understand what you want it to do. twice a match between.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah, sounds really complicated. Like, uh, I mean, it, it sounds like, uh, it touches different, um, fields. So you need to write, uh, first design what the system is gonna look like. I'm sure like there might be some 3D modeling in there or like circuiting, circuit designs in there. And then probably you also need to write some code on how the you know, different components, uh, interact. And then is, is there some hardware also involved? Do you have to also like, you know, actually build the hardware components and test this out? It sounds interesting, but at the same time it sounds also very, very complex.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: With embedded systems, it's great to have the idea or knowledge of what 3D design is. It's great to have an idea of electrical wiring stuff. It's great to have an idea of building hardware. However, how that looks to you as an embedded systems engineer depends on where you are working, depends on the company you're working with, and it also depends on your role in that company. Currently, in the company that I'm working at, we have groups of people who come up with the idea for how this machine should operate, and then we have systems engineers who work with mechanical engineers to decide, okay, is this is the 3D model, this is how we want it to physically look and how we want it to physically move. Systems engineers would also interact with electrical teams to decide, okay, well, we're going to have harnessing this way, this is how our various sensors are going to behave, and this is the feedback we need to be able to work on code. And then systems engineers would interact with the software engineers, which is where I would come in. That's my current role. So I work as an embedded systems engineer. I work mostly on the software that would interact with all of these 3 areas of the system, and then I also get the opportunity to go out and actually test it out on machines.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So, um, you mentioned like in your current company there are different roles, and I'm curious like what's, you know, the organizational structure or like team structure for you know, your role typically is, it's, do you, can you give me like a glimpse of, you know, what someone should expect or what they would expect like when they go first go into their first role as an embedded systems engineer in a company like yours?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: I think you should definitely expect to do some kind of programming and you should definitely expect to encounter concepts in embedded systems like concurrency, understanding how the general system works, which you shouldn't necessarily know how it works immediately because it's not your design, but you can interact with people, you can interact with documents and read and understand how these parts should interact with each other to design your code according to what you have available. So I guess if you're looking for an opportunity to work as an embedded systems engineer, You do need some programming. Um, and it helps to know some circuitry. It also helps to know a bit of like mechanical design, not in depth, but having an idea of both of those makes it easier to work on embedded systems. Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: With the programming, are there like, uh, specific programming languages that you need to know? 'Cause I remember back in school, like, um, in computing or engineering class, uh, we did some kind of like Arduino programming. I imagine like you might use some form of high-level programming as well, uh, or is this gonna be like low-level programming stuff? What kind of programming languages or programming do you do in this particular role?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Programming languages that you can use in this role, it varies again depending on the company you're at. Some people use C++, some people use C. Um, I'm actually glad you brought up Arduino because That is like a small-scale representation of what it's like working as an embedded systems engineer. You write some code or you build some code and then you flash it onto the Arduino and then you get to test it out and see if it behaves the way that you want it to. It's just in embedded systems rules, it becomes a maximized form of that same situation. So while I have like a microcontroller for my Arduino, now I'm just gonna have a controller. I'm just gonna have a much bigger bigger controller. I'm just gonna have much higher voltages coming out. Depending on what kind of controller your company decides to use, that can determine what languages you guys are gonna be programming in. Some companies would like to go straight ahead and code in C++ and spend the time building it and then sending it away onto the controller and testing it out. Some people would also like to use something I'm— I guess a lot of people have become familiar with recently is MATLAB. MathWorks MATLAB Simulink. It has the ability also to compile code for you when you have made your Simulink structures, and then you would have C code that you can actually flash to a controller and then get tested, get stuff tested. I think it has support for Arduino as well, so it really depends. But if you are able to pick a standard programming language that is used in embedded, which I would say either C or C++, and then you have a good understanding of how sensors work, or how, how to read parts documents, or how to read documents that describe how a sensor works, or how a particular feature that you're adding to your machine works, it makes a lot of difference. It helps a lot. But really, if you have good communication skills, and then if you have a solid programming language and you're able to read these part documents, I think you're on your way. You're on fast track to get an opportunity in the embedded world.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Oh, sounds, um, still sounds like a bit of, you know, you, you need to have a solid background in, and I guess like you need to have some form of like, uh, engineering background.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Um, probably electronics engineering or I don't know what majors you need to, you know, have to be able to go into to like this role? Like, is there any particular major? And I don't imagine like with, you know, this particular field you can just go to a bootcamp. I don't even know if they have bootcamps for these, but I imagine like you have to have a CS major or something. Like what majors do you need to, to, to know?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Actually, I think if I were listing them, I'd probably say, because I did electrical and electronics engineering at Ashesi, I would say that would be like number one, but that's just because I did it. Electrical electronics engineering, and then I would say mechanical engineering is helpful, so maybe mechanical engineering. And then I'd probably go from electrical electronics to computer engineering and then mechanical engineering. I think computer science is helpful But it depends on how you were taught or what you got to do in whatever college you go to, because some colleges have made it possible so that if you're doing computer science, you can also do some things in the field of electronics. You can get the feel of how to use electronics and stuff like that. But some also focus mainly on like algorithms and data structures and everything computer scientists are so interested in. Um, but definitely knowing some software and knowing some electronics is like central to the idea. So if, if you have the opportunity to learn, I would, I would say the easiest thing for me was learning embedded C. And people talk about C or C# or C++ being like super complicated and everything. I really think you can read a book and do it. Um, There are countless books out there, so you can just look at them. There's a lot of open-source coding sites that you can practice on. And then once you have a feel of just being able to program basic things in C, because again, you don't want something overly complex and making your controller's brain just not be able to process what you're doing fast enough to get the actions you want. So learn the basics of C, and then then you can look at using an Arduino. And rather than using the already existing libraries of the Arduino, you can try to create your own libraries for how components should work. So that would be like, I guess, a scaled-down version. So if you're able to learn C basics of C, and then using an Arduino going over. the existing library code first, you'd be able to tell, okay, this is actually very similar to what I just did in learning just C. After understanding how that works, it would be nice to try to recreate those in C without using the existing libraries. And after figuring that out, or at least during the process of figuring that out, you'd realize that, okay, to be able to do this, I actually need to know how this LED works, so I need to know how this buzzer works. So I need to know how these, you know, components, all the little things that come with the Arduino kits, you'd need to figure out how to search them up on the internet, find their part numbers and search them up and understand, okay, these are what these pins mean. This is how to interpret what comes through here. This is how to read this voltage, then you can move ahead to a controller that is not as popular or doesn't have preexisting libraries. So one of the controllers that I used in school was the Freedom Board. It has an ARM controller, which a lot of companies are really excited to see on your resume. If you mention that you have worked with an ARM controller, an ARM-based controller, they would be very impressed. And if you're able to explain how you used it to make whatever projects that you have created. It really helps. So in using something like that, because it doesn't have documented libraries on, okay, well, this is how to use an LED with this controller, this is how to send code and then have a buzzer do this sequence of beats and everything, you'd figure it out. And being able to figure that out by searching on the information of these components and how this controller works and what these lights mean on this board Mm-hmm. Is a very important skill to have. And if you're able to do that, you'd be able to do a lot of work in the embedded world because that's what I did and that was the only background that I had. And I did my interview and I'm able to do my work every day.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Now about, uh, interviews and like what a job search is like for, you know, embedded system roles. What's the interview process like?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Again, it varies from company to company. I've worked in an embedded systems role in 2 different companies. In one company, um, they stuck to the regular looking at your resume. Being able to clearly articulate that, okay, this is how this part works, this is how this other part works, and to be able to get clean code, to be able to get code that actually makes sense to try and implement in the real world. I try to explore on creating my own personal libraries for how this thing is going to work. A thing that people are also concerned about is how much space you're gonna have on that controller's memory. So you want to write code that definitely covers the functionality of each component, but covers just the functionality that you need or is necessary that you have space for to be able to put all of that on the controller and have all the features that you want to be working together interact with each other. So knowing your project, but also knowing keywords that embedded systems engineers would be looking for.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: They would want to hear things like the controller's— the actual ID for the controller. Like, do you know what is on this board, or are you just calling it a Freedom board? And then given that information about the controller, do you think that these components that you're interacting with the controller with— or do you, do you know your hardware pinouts as well to be able to visualize that, okay, if I'm gonna need all of these pinouts, then I'm going to use this number of pinouts in a way that would make my project look less complicated, or I'll have enough pins with this board to be able to do the project that I want to do and still have it working right, but also looking good and also working like as fast as I would need it to. So you need to know the keywords to, to mention, and it would also be great for you to be able to tell them about protocols that you have encountered while you are learning or while you were making your project. Is I2C. In real systems, I work on vehicles, so in a lot of these systems, one of the main network protocols you'd want to have an idea of is CAN. CAN networks are very, very important. They're used in like every vehicle, so it's great to have an idea of how that works. And even if you haven't interacted with CAN, it's just great to know about it, be able to identify it, so that in an interview you can say, okay, I haven't interacted with it, but I know this is what it does, this is how to interact with it, this is how to use it. And based on that alone, you should be able to pick it up in an office setting. In other interviews, there's also the STAR method, them just expecting that you have good communication skills, you're able to tell them how you've handled an issue in a very decent way that they feel like, okay, our company is actually going to be able to have you on our team, actually able to work with someone like you. So you need to have a good balance between the two because one of the interviews was more skewed towards what I had done or what I have done on my resume and And so you need to know every bit of it. They don't want a situation where it's like, oh, you wrote this project, and then they ask you and you're like, oh yeah, um, for this project, and then you give a summary of it like you don't actually know what happened in the project. And they also want someone who's like a real person and can tell you, okay, I've encountered a situation like this and this is what has happened. So the STAR method and really knowing your project.
